content.value: Trace nested decisions and else-if chains; choose branch order and use braces to show which else belongs to which if.

Nested selection puts a decision inside another branch. Evaluate outer conditions first: a skipped outer branch means its inner conditions are not evaluated. An else-if chain is a convenient way to select one of several cases, with the first matching test taking precedence.

Order conditions from the cases that must be recognized first toward more general fallbacks. For descending score thresholds, test the highest threshold before lower ones. A final else covers all remaining cases. Explicit braces make nesting clear because Java otherwise associates else with the nearest unmatched if, not with indentation.
85 fails the first condition and satisfies the second, so grade becomes B. The final else is skipped. If the >= 80 test came first, a score of 95 would incorrectly be assigned B by that branch.
Do not treat an else-if chain as a collection of independent ifs. Changing braces can alter which fallback executes. Include tests that exercise every branch and the exact threshold values.
For the worked example, predict grades for 79, 80, 89, and 90: Below B, B, B, A. Then describe how an outer valid-score test could reject negative inputs before this chain.
